ideas.name: outboard_rack_slide
ideas.description: A long-travel slide jaw. The moving carriage rides two 3 x 150 mm steel rods on LM3UU bushings, like long_slide. Unlike long_slide, the module-1 rack is fixed to the carriage's outboard face, on the side away from the fixed jaw. The printed gear sector (pitch radius 49.6 mm, so 49.6 mm of finger travel per servo radian) meshes with it from the outboard side. When the jaw opens the rack extends outward, beyond the hand. When it closes the rack moves outward too, never into the space above the grasp gap. No drive member sits inside the gap at any opening, so the clearance above an object is limited only by the arm, not by a rack about 39–64 mm above the fingertips as on the stock long_slide. The moving finger is a straight vertical PLA blade, 40 mm below the carriage, with a 1 mm TPU face (friction 0.9). The fixed jaw gets a matching straight blade pad, so neither fingertip curves inward over an object's top. Faces stay parallel (0 deg) and the tip stays level (+1 mm) at every opening, from 17 mm (dice) to about 93 mm (sugar box).

ideas.name: pivoting_self_aligning_pad
ideas.description: A printed PLA pad carrier, 24 mm tall and 12–16 mm wide, with a 1 mm TPU skin (μ 0.9). It hangs on a horizontal pin through the bottom of the stock moving jaw: an M3 screw running in two MR63 bearings, pin 6 mm above the pad's lower edge, reach 0. ideas.name: geared_high_rack_slide
ideas.description: A long slide with the rack lifted out of the gap. Two 3x150 mm steel rods in two LM3UU bushings carry the carriage, mounted level with the gripper servo axis, about 80 mm above the fingertips. A printed module-1 gear of 40 teeth (20 mm pitch radius) on the servo horn drives a printed compound idler on a 3 mm steel axle in two MR63 bearings. The idler's 20-tooth gear meshes the horn gear, and its 50-tooth gear drives the rack from below, with the rack teeth facing down. Finger travel is 20*(25/10) = 50 mm per servo radian, so about 96 mm over -0.17..1.75 rad. Squeeze is 1.62 N*m / 0.050 m = 32 N, about 29 N after mesh losses, enough for the 514 g sugar box (2*0.5*29 = 29 N against about 7.5 N with lift margin). The finger hangs from the carriage on a straight printed drop leg about 80 mm long. Its face stays vertical and its tip does not rise at any opening, and it carries the existing 2 mm TPU pads with pad_angle 0 and reach 0. The only part crossing the gap is the carriage itself, about 75 mm above the fingertip, so tall objects grasped at their equator (tomato 68 lying) or near the top (potted 84 upright, grasped shallow) are not touched. Added wrist mass is about 90 g, which puts the shoulder at about 0.41 + 0.77 (sugar) + 0.14 = 1.32 N*m against a 1.62 N*m stall.

proposals.edit: jaw -> long_slide (sector_radius_mm=50)
proposals.mechanism: moving_jaw_on_top_face (pudding_box, sugar_box, mustard_bottle, tuna_fish_can) and squeezed_down_out (gelatin_box). Both come from the hinged jaw. It swings on an 81 mm radius, so at wide openings the fingertip rises and the face tilts. The brief gives +14 mm and 44 deg at 75 mm, and +23 mm and 53 deg at 85 mm. The tips rise above low box tops: tuna top +17 vs tip +18 to +22, pudding top +19 vs tip +15 to +23, sugar top +23 vs tip +18 to +22. The contact then presses on the top face at 73 to 85 deg down. On the gelatin box (73 mm) the face sits 33 deg down: tan 33 = 0.65, above the bare PLA friction of 0.45, so the box squeezes out downward.
proposals.principle: Two contacts hold an object only if their normals are horizontal and opposed, and the fingertip must reach below the object's top. A finger that slides straight along the closing axis neither turns nor rises as it opens.
proposals.hypothesis: long_slide at sector_radius_mm=50 opens to 103 mm, enough for the widest failing object (mustard bottle, 96 mm). The brief gives face -0 deg and tip +1 mm at 35, 55 and 85 mm, with 32 N squeeze, more than today's 20 N. So every failing object gets antipodal side contacts below its top. The heaviest case, the sugar box (514 g, 5.0 N), has 2*0.5*32 = 32 N of friction capacity. The shoulder needs about 0.41 + 0.15*5.14 = 1.18 N*m, below the 1.62 N*m stall, which leaves margin for the slide's extra mass. Cheaper moves cannot fix this. No pad_angle keeps the hinge both parallel and low across 17 to 96 mm: at 45 deg the tip is still +14 mm at 85 mm, and the face is -21 deg at 35 mm. The parallelogram at 90 mm still lifts the tip +33 mm at 85 mm. Prismatic tops out at 68 mm, which would drop apple and banana. Cost: $6.40 (2 lm3uu + 2 rods 3x150), 3 days, 216 machine minutes, all within the $40, 7 day and 600 minute limits.
risks: Round objects (golf_ball, apple, lemon, plum, strawberry, racquetball, tennis_ball, tomato_soup_can) now meet two flat parallel faces with no centring. If the grasp height misses the equator they could roll out. They should survive: the contacts stay horizontal and the tip stays at +1 mm at every width, so System 1 can set depth to the equator, and squeeze rises from 20 to 32 N.
Small objects (dice 17 mm, large_marker 19 mm): with a 50 mm/rad sector, closing resolution is coarser. The minimum opening is still about 7 mm (103 - 96 mm of travel), so both remain reachable.
potted_meat_can (370 g, friction 0.35): needs 2*0.35*N > 3.6 N with margin. At 32 N this improves on today.
Added wrist mass (43 g PLA plus rods) slightly raises shoulder torque. It is still well under stall.

iterations.notes:
I put two changes forward for trial: swap the hinged jaw for the long slide, and add TPU-faced pads.

**What is failing.** Every failure traces back to the hinged jaw. It swings on an 81 mm radius, so at wide openings the moving fingertip rises: +14 mm at 75 mm and +23 mm at 85 mm. The low wide boxes and cans have tops at +17 to +23 mm, so the jaw ends up pressing on the top face instead of the side. The gelatin box is the milder case: its contact sits 33 deg down, and bare PLA friction (0.45) is below tan 33 deg (0.65), so the box squeezes out downward.

**Proposal 1: replace the hinged jaw with the long slide (sector radius 50 mm).**
- **Why this part:** it is the only catalogue jaw that keeps the face flat and the fingertip at +1 mm while opening wide enough (up to 103 mm) for the mustard bottle (96 mm). Squeeze rises to 32 N.
- **What to buy:** 2 lm3uu linear bushings ($1.20 each) and 2 steel rods 3x150 mm ($2 each). That is $6.40, 3 days lead time and 216 machine minutes, all within the $40, 7-day and 600-minute limits.
- **Why not the alternatives:**
  - The 12 V servos are refused on budget, and the arm already has torque margin even for the 514 g sugar box (about 1.18 of 1.62 N*m).
  - Prismatic tops out at 68 mm, which would lose the apple and banana.
  - Parallelogram still lifts the tip +33 mm at 85 mm.
  - No pad angle keeps the hinged jaw both parallel and low across 17 to 96 mm.
- **Main risk:** the round objects now meet two flat parallel faces. They should hold at the equator with the higher squeeze, but the trial decides.

**Proposal 2: TPU-faced pads (free) to save the gelatin box if the slide fails.**
- **Settings:** 2 mm TPU skin, 10 deg pad tilt, no extra reach.
- **Why it could work:** TPU friction of 0.9 beats tan 33 deg (0.65), so the gelatin box's tilted contact should hold.
- **Why the settings:** no extra reach, because a longer pad raises the fingertip further. The small tilt is safe with or without the slide.
- **Limits:** it will not fix the contacts on top faces (73 to 85 deg).
- **Main risk:** the small objects (dice, marker, wood cube) meet a slightly tilted face at narrow openings, which the higher friction should tolerate.

If neither change gains a group, the next step is a groove for the round objects on the slide.

proposals.principle: A fingertip on a swinging joint rises by about R(1-cos q). On the hinge, the moving pad's face is parallel to the fixed face at the opening equal to pad_angle. iterations.notes:
I've sent three body changes for trial. All three swap the hinged jaw for the long slide and remove the printed pads, at three gear-sector radii: 46, 44 and 42 mm. Each costs $6.40 (two linear bushings and two 3 x 150 mm steel rods), 3 days and 216 machine minutes, well inside the $40 left. The main risk is that the interference check refuses all three before any trial, as it did at 50 and 48 mm.

**Why a slide:** the four failing objects are wide and low, and the hinged jaw can't hold them by their sides:
- **Tuna can (85 mm):** at that opening the moving fingertip sits 29 mm above the fixed one, and the face tilts 52 degrees.
- **Pudding box (90 mm):** the moving pad presses down on the top face (30 N at 87 degrees down), and the fixed jaw never touches it.
- **Sugar box (92 mm) and mustard bottle (96 mm):** the hinged jaw opens only 90 mm. The moving pad also ended on the top face in the runs where it touched.

Three trials of pad settings gained nothing. The parallelogram jaw is worse (+48 mm at 85 mm), and the rack-and-pinion slide opens only 58 mm. The long slide is the only catalogue part whose fingers neither turn nor rise.

**Why these radii:** at 50 and 48 mm the gear sector overlapped the wrist by under half a millimetre at the jaw's closed limit (-0.17 rad), so I step the radius down. The 1.6 mm-per-radian link between radius and opening is my reading of the 30 mm and 50 mm entries in the catalogue, not a computed fact. Removing the pads gives back about 9–10 mm of opening, and a slide doesn't need the 10-degree pad tilt.

| Radius | Expected opening | Squeeze | Should gain |
|---|---|---|---|
| 46 mm | about 96 mm | about 35 N | all four, mustard at the limit; most likely to clash |
| 44 mm | about 92.5 mm | about 37 N | tuna, pudding, likely sugar (tight) |
| 42 mm | about 89 mm | about 39 N | tuna only; mainly a test of where the clash stops |

**Held objects at risk:** removing the pads drops face friction from 0.9 to 0.45.
- The heavy metal cans should still hold, because the squeeze nearly doubles from 20 N.
- The gelatin box no longer needs the extra grip, because the faces are now parallel.
- The rolling objects already pass with flat faces, and flat faces that don't rise should hold them more cleanly.
- The higher squeeze on light objects (dice, cup, strawberry) depends on System 1 tuning how far the jaw closes.
- Arm load with the sugar box is about 1.27 N·m, below the 1.62 N·m stall.

If all three are refused, the next step is the recorded spacer-offset version of the slide, since no smaller radius reaches these widths.

proposals.edit: pads -> pads (groove_mm=0, lip_mm=0, pad_angle_deg=0, pad_tpu_mm=1, reach_mm=20, width_mm=12)
proposals.mechanism: Failing groups: moving_jaw_on_top_face and fixed_jaw_missed. The revolute tip rises +20 to +29 mm at 76–85 mm and the face tilts 42–52°, and the jaw opens no wider than 90 mm. The long_slide fixes this; b03t4 gains pudding, sugar, tuna and mustard. Its own losses come from two other mechanisms. (a) Rack or carriage on the object's top: on the banana, 'rack pressed 5 N down on its top', closure stopped at 80 mm on a 70 mm banana. On tomato, 'rack pressed 8 N down', stopped at 78 mm on a 68 mm can. On potted meat, 'carriage pressed 30 N on its side at +42 (top at +42)'. (b) slipped_under_load on potted meat: 33–36 N squeeze on bare PLA faces against 0.35 metal.
proposals.principle: A finger holds an object's side only if the fingertip reaches below the object's top while the rest of the hand clears it. On a slide the finger does not rotate, so extending it adds no tip rise (the tip stays at +1 mm at every opening). The extension therefore lifts the rack and carriage by reach_mm relative to the grasp point and gives up nothing. TPU (friction 0.9) instead of bare PLA (0.45) restores the friction that held potted meat on the current body. On a slide, pad_angle 0 keeps the faces parallel. The current 10° value is what puts the slide's face at -10°.
proposals.hypothesis: The interference law accepted b03t4 (long_slide r=49.6), so no clash. Its bare opening is about 102 mm, interpolating the brief's 103 mm at r=50. Pads at about 4 mm per face with a 1 mm TPU skin leave about 94 mm, which covers tuna (85), pudding (90) and sugar (92). Mustard (96) probably drops out. Squeeze is 1.62/0.0496 ≈ 33 N. 2·0.5·33 = 33 N against the 5.0 N sugar weight; 2·0.35·33 = 23 N against the 3.6 N potted meat. Arm load at 514 g is 0.41 + 0.77 = 1.18 N·m, under the 1.62 N·m stall. A 20 mm reach raises the rack and carriage 20 mm above the grasp height. That should clear the banana top (+19) and the tomato top, and it lets the carriage pass over the potted meat can's top edge instead of hitting it. Pads alone cannot do this: three pad-only trials on the revolute gained nothing, because the hinge's rise is the limit there. Cost: $6.40 for 2 lm3uu bushings and 2 rods of 3×150 mm; screws on hand; 3 days; about 216 + 25 = 241 machine minutes.
risks: mustard_bottle stays failing: 96 mm is wider than the ~94 mm left once the pads are on
banana / tomato_soup_can: if the rack sits more than 20 mm too low, it still hits their tops. System 1's depth tuning and the follow-up reach fit should cover this
dice / large_marker / wood_block_cube: longer fingers on the smallest objects. The faces stay parallel and the minimum gap only shrinks, so these should hold
round objects (golf, plum, strawberry, tennis, racquetball, apple, lemon): parallel flat faces with no groove, the same as the bare-slide trials, which held all of them

- **20–30 mm reach:** the fingertips extend below the rack and carriage. On a slide this costs no tip rise.
- **A TPU skin:** friction 0.9 instead of 0.45.

iterations.notes:
Diagnosis. All four failing objects are wide and low: tuna 85 mm wide × 34 mm tall, pudding 90 × 38, sugar 92 × 45, mustard 96 × 58. The cause is the stock revolute jaw itself. At the openings these objects need, its moving fingertip rises above the fixed one: +12 mm at 65 mm, +19 mm at 75 mm, +29 mm at 85 mm. Its face also tilts 34–52°. So the moving pad comes down on the top face, as the logs show: 30 N pushing 87° down, with the contact at +18 mm and the object top at +19 mm. The widest opening is only 90 mm, short of pudding, sugar and mustard.

Pad settings can't fix this on the hinge. Even pad_angle 45 leaves +14° tilt and +14 mm rise at 85 mm. It would also tilt the faces about −21° or more at 17–35 mm, which tips dice, marker and wood cube out upward (tan 21° ≈ 0.38, close to their friction of 0.4).

Of the catalogue parts, only the slide keeps the face level and the fingertip from rising (0° tilt, +1 mm at every opening). Trials b031, b03t2 and b03t4 confirm it gains pudding, sugar and tuna, and mustard too at r ≥ 46.7. The 12 V servos are refused on budget and the arm torque is not the limit (1.18 of 1.62 N·m with the sugar box).

The slide's losses follow a pattern. Bare, the rack lands on the banana with 1 mm overlap (pressing at +20 mm, top at +19), and it lost potted meat and tomato soup. With 20 mm pad reach, the banana problem goes away, but the potted meat (84 mm tall) is hit on the approach; at reach 30, apple, cup and tennis ball are hit as well. So the reach window is somewhere between about 2 and 15 mm. Pad width and TPU thickness inside that window are untested.

The three proposals sit in that gap, so they don't repeat a past trial. Each builds on a slide base and costs $6.40 from the manifest (2 × lm3uu, 2 × 150 mm rods), 3 days and about 240 machine minutes. I'm least sure about tomato soup: every slide variant at r ≥ 44 has lost it, and my explanation (the carriage or rack hits first) is an inference, not something read off the simulator.

iterations.notes:
Diagnosis. On the stock hinge, all four failing objects fail for the same reason: the jaw doesn't open wide enough and its tip rises too much. The pads opening is at most 90 mm, which is less than pudding 90, sugar 92 and mustard 96. So the moving jaw starts above these objects and lands on the top face: 30 N pushing 87 deg down at +18 mm with the top at +19. Tuna (85 mm) fits inside 90 mm, but at 85 mm the moving tip sits +29 mm above the fixed one, and the pad pressed on the 34 mm-tall tuna's top (+16, top at +17).

Iterations 5 and 6 tried the long_slide many times. It removes the tip rise, but its rack and carriage hit tall and lying objects: banana (rack on top at +20, top +19), tomato soup (stopped with no contact at 1.41 rad, 78 mm, in every variant), and potted meat. Pad reach could not clear 68–84 mm-tall objects without losing apple, cup and tennis ball at reach 30. I am not repeating it.

The cheapest lever not yet used is the moving pad's tilt on the hinge. The brief says that going from pad_angle 10 to 45 deg moves the widest opening from 90 to 95 mm, cuts the tip rise at 85 mm from +29 to +14 mm, and cuts the face tilt at 85 mm from +52 to +14 deg. Thinning the TPU skin from 2 to 0.5 mm should add about 3 mm of opening (the bare faces reach 99 mm) and keep friction at 0.9.

The trade-off is small objects: at 35 mm, pad_angle 45 tilts the face -21 deg (bottom swung in) with the tip 10 mm low. So I bracket the angle at 28, 36 and 45 deg. All three are parameter moves that cost one print (about 2 g PLA and 1 g TPU, about 18 min) and no money. Nothing needs buying. The 12 V servos are still too expensive at $68 against $40 left, and the arm doesn't need them: holding sugar takes 0.41 + 0.15×5.14 ≈ 1.18 N·m, under the 1.62 N·m stall.

proposals.mechanism: There are two mechanisms, one per jaw family. (1) On the hinged jaw it is moving_jaw_on_top_face, which comes from the opening limit. The brief gives fingertips at most 90 mm apart. Pudding (90 mm), sugar (92) and mustard (96) are at or beyond that limit. At 85 mm (tuna) the moving tip sits +29 mm above the fixed one and the face is tilted +52 deg, so the pad lands on the top face (87 deg down, 30 N). (2) On long_slide, the only catalogue jaw whose tip stays at +1 mm and whose face stays flat out to about 93-97 mm, the slide hardware (carriage, rack and rods) sits low, roughly 40-45 mm above the fingertip, and pokes inboard of the finger face. That hits tall or round objects before the fingers close. The record shows it: the carriage pressed 30 N on the potted meat's side at +42 mm (b03t2). The rack pressed down on the banana's top at +20 mm, 1 mm into its 38 mm height (b031, b051). Tomato soup stopped at 78 mm apart with neither jaw touching (every long_slide body). At about 45 mm above the table the lying 68 mm can is still about 62-65 mm wide, so the inboard carriage meets it about 10 mm before the finger does. Tomato soup has been lost on every one of the 13+ long_slide trials, whatever the sector radius or pad settings.
proposals.principle: A finger can only hold an object's side if it reaches below the object's top with clearance. That clearance must hold for every part that moves with the finger, not just the fingertip. Every part above the fingertip that sits inside the closing gap shortens the finger that can be used. A straight slide fixes the tip-rise (R(1-cos q)) and face-tilt problems. Its hardware must sit above the tallest object (the 84 mm potted meat can) and outboard of the face plane.
proposals.hypothesis:
The catalogue is used up for these four groups. Five pads parameter trials gained nothing; they bracketed pad_angle at 28, 36 and 45 deg and lost the banana at 36 and 45. Parallelogram still swings its tip on a circle (+48 mm at 85 mm with link 90). Prismatic opens to at most 58 mm. servos_12v costs $68 against the $40 left and does not address grip geometry. Every long_slide variant gains pudding, sugar and tuna (and mustard when bare) but loses tomato soup, plus potted meat or banana depending on the reach setting. The cause is where the slide's hardware sits, not the sector radius or the pads, and no catalogue parameter moves it.

The proposed part is a long slide with a drop finger. The rods and carriage are raised so their lowest point is at least 90 mm above the fingertip, above the 84 mm potted meat can. The carriage sits outboard of (behind) the moving face plane, so no part of it ever enters the gap. The moving finger is an L-shaped printed drop, 90 mm long with a 12 x 14 mm section. Under 35 N its tip deflects about F L^3/(3EI) = 35*90^3/(3*3500*2016) ≈ 1.2 mm. The fixed jaw gets a matching 90 mm face so the faces stay antipodal. The gear sector is offset from the wrist roll, as in the recorded long_slide_offset_sector idea, so r=50 no longer interferes. The design takes sector radius 46 mm: squeeze 1.62/0.046 ≈ 35 N, travel 46 x 1.92 rad ≈ 88 mm, and with thin 0.5 mm TPU faces the opening reaches about 96-97 mm. Grip margin on the heaviest failing object: sugar 514 g gives 2 x 0.5 x 35 = 35 N against 5 N. The added mass at the wrist is about 25 g, about +0.04 N*m at the shoulder. With sugar held that is 0.41 + 0.77 + 0.04 ≈ 1.22 N*m, under the 1.62 N*m stall.
risks: tomato_soup_can, potted_meat_can and banana: these are the groups every long_slide body lost, and this design is aimed at them. They survive only if the hardware truly stays above 90 mm and outboard of the face.

dice and large_marker (17-19 mm): a 90 mm finger has a longer moment arm for wrist-roll and approach collisions. The slide's flat face and +1 mm tip are kinder to small objects than the hinge's -21 deg face at pad_angle 45.
potted_meat_can slip: squeeze drops from about 37 N (r=44, which held it) to 35 N, still 2 x 0.35 x 35 = 24.5 N against 3.6 N.
the interference law: a taller, longer finger sweeps more volume around the wrist roll and must pass the no-interference check.

idea.name: long_slide_drop_finger
idea.description: A straight-travel moving jaw. A printed module-1 gear sector (pitch radius 46 mm) on the gripper servo horn, offset clear of the wrist roll, drives a rack on a carriage that rides two 3 x 150 mm ground steel rods on LM3UU bushings. The rods and carriage are mounted at least 90 mm above the fingertips and wholly outboard of the moving finger's face plane, so no slide hardware enters the gap between the jaws at any opening. The moving finger is a printed L-shaped drop link, 90 mm long with a 12 x 14 mm section, hanging from the carriage. It carries the existing pad (0.5 mm TPU skin, 0 deg, 12 mm wide). A matching 90 mm printed extension on the fixed jaw keeps the two faces vertical and opposed. The finger neither turns nor rises (tip about +1 mm at every opening). The opening is about 96-97 mm and the squeeze about 35 N.
idea.test: Add a long_slide variant to the simulator with two new geometry parameters: carriage_height_mm (the lowest point of the rods, carriage and rack above the fingertip, range 40-100) and carriage_inset_mm (how far the carriage sits behind the face plane, at least 0). Add a fixed-jaw extension of the same drop length. Run the interference check over the wrist-roll range and the full servo range -0.17..1.75 rad. Then run the full 21-object suite at sector_radius_mm 46, carriage_height_mm 90 and carriage_inset_mm 3. Watch tomato_soup_can (does it close to 68 mm and touch both jaws?), potted_meat_can (no carriage contact at +42 mm) and banana (no rack contact).

iterations.notes:
I'm not proposing a test this time, because I couldn't find a catalogue change with a real chance of being kept. The only proposal is a new part (an "idea"), so the simulator won't trial it.

- **Stock hinged jaw:** five pad-parameter trials gained nothing. The jaw opens to 90 mm at most, so the pudding (90), sugar (92) and mustard (96) can't fit. On the tuna (85) the moving fingertip rises 29 mm above the fixed one.
- **Straight long slide:** this is the only catalogue jaw that keeps the fingertip level and the face flat. It lost tomato soup in all 13+ trials, and lost potted meat or banana depending on pad reach. The record shows why: its carriage and rack sit about 40-45 mm above the fingertip and stick into the gap between the jaws.
  - It pressed 30 N on the potted meat's side.
  - It pressed down on the banana's top, 1 mm into it.
  - It stopped about 10 mm short on the lying tomato can, with neither jaw touching.
- **Other parts:** no sector radius or pad setting moves that hardware. Repeating those trials would only lose the same groups again. The 12 V servos cost $68 against the $40 left, and they wouldn't fix the grip geometry anyway.

The new part is a long slide with a 90 mm drop finger. The rods and carriage sit above the tallest object (the 84 mm potted meat can) and behind the moving finger's face, so nothing but the faces enters the gap. It reuses the recorded idea of offsetting the gear sector so it clears the wrist.

What to buy: 2 LM3UU bearings and 2 steel rods 3 x 150 mm. That's $6.40, 3 days' lead time and about 283 machine minutes. Everything else is already on hand.

proposals.edit: pads (groove_mm=0, lip_mm=0, pad_angle_deg=10, pad_tpu_mm=2, reach_mm=30, width_mm=12)
proposals.mechanism: moving_jaw_on_top_face on pudding, sugar and mustard, plus force_limit on tuna and fixed_jaw_missed on its regrasp. The brief puts the widest opening at 90 mm, and these objects are 90, 92 and 96 mm wide, so the jaw cannot open past them. The moving pad lands on the top face (30 N 'pushing 87 deg down' at +18 mm, top at +19). Tuna is 85 mm wide, so it fits, but at that width the moving tip is +29 mm above the fixed one with only 34 mm of object height, so it presses the top (7 N at +16, top at +17).
proposals.principle: A fingertip on a swinging joint opens by about R sin(dq) and rises by about R(1 - cos dq). For a set opening, a longer radius needs a smaller angle, so the rise falls roughly as width^2/(2R) and the face tilts less. The widest opening grows with R. Squeeze is servo torque over the lever, 1.62/R.
proposals.hypothesis: No pads parameter tried in the record changes R; the five trials only moved pad_angle. reach_mm has never been raised on the revolute jaw in the record, and it is the one parameter that lengthens the swing radius. Fitting the brief's table gives this model: tip vertical at q=0.24 rad (25 mm); opening ≈ 25 + R sin(q-0.24); rise ≈ R(1-cos); R=81 mm gives 85.8 mm and +27.5 mm at 1.09 rad, against the brief's 85 and +29. Face angle ≈ q - pad_angle, which matches 11, 18, 26 and 52 deg. With reach 30 (R≈111): widest opening ≈ 25 + 111·sin(0.96) ≈ 116 mm, so mustard at 96 now fits. Tuna at 85 mm: rise +18 mm, face 37 deg. Pudding at 90: +18 mm, 40 deg. Sugar at 92: +20 mm, 41 deg. Mustard at 96: +23 mm (58 tall), 43 deg. That is the geometry gelatin_box already holds under now (73 mm at R=81: +16 mm, 40 deg, 30 mm tall). Tuna is the tightest: about 11 mm of tip below its 34 mm top, and mu 0.35 at 171 g. Squeeze falls to about 14.6 N; for sugar, 2·0.5·14.6 = 14.6 N against 5.0 N of weight. Arm load for sugar: 0.41 + 0.15·5.14 = 1.18 N·m, under the 1.62 stall. Nothing to buy; it is a reprint of the pads (PLA and TPU, on hand), about 40 machine minutes.
risks: potted_meat_can and tomato_soup_can: squeeze drops from 20 to about 14.6 N. 2·0.35·14.6 = 10.2 N against 3.6 N of weight leaves about 2.8x margin, so they should hold. The narrower faces (57 mm: face 20 deg instead of 27) help too.

dice, large_marker: at 17 mm the face comes out about 0 deg instead of 2 deg bottom-in, and the tip rise about 0.3 mm. That is no worse than now, but the fixed pad being 30 mm longer changes the approach depth System 1 must find.

banana, gelatin_box, apple: these get flatter faces and lower tips (banana at 70 mm: face 28 deg instead of 37, rise 9.5 instead of 14 mm), so they should survive. The wrist rides 30 mm higher, which slightly changes the arm pose during the lift.

On the revolute jaw the moving fingertip swings on a circle about 81 mm in radius, so it rises above the fixed one: +29 mm at 85 mm, with the face 52 deg off parallel, and the widest opening is 90 mm. On the only catalogue part that opens wide and flat (long_slide), the rack and sector pass over the gap and press on tall objects (tomato_soup_can, banana). Long pad reach then lands the pads on the tops of tall objects (potted_meat_can, apple).
proposals.principle: A finger can hold an object's side only if, at that object's opening, it reaches below the object's top with clearance. Likewise, nothing that moves with the drive may pass through the space above the object lower than that object's top. Two contacts must be antipodal: a face that stays vertical, with a tip that does not rise.
proposals.hypothesis: The record shows the catalogue is used up for these four groups. (1) Revolute pads: 8 parameter trials gained 0 groups. The best geometry, pad_angle 45, gives a +14 deg face and a +14 mm tip at 85 mm but loses the banana (iterations 3, 7). The widest opening of 90–98 mm is still below the sugar box (92) and mustard bottle (96) plus clearance. (2) Parallelogram swings its tip by +48 mm at 85 mm. Prismatic opens only 58 mm. (3) long_slide gains pudding, sugar, tuna and sometimes mustard on every body tried (b031, b03t2, b03t4, b040, b05t1), and it loses tomato_soup_can on every body tried: sector 44 to 49.6, reach 0 to 26. Reach 26 adds 21 mm: at most 60 mm. Reach 30, the top of the range, gives at most 64 mm. The lying tomato can is 68 mm tall. Iteration 10 logged 'rack pressed 7 N down on its top at +33 (top +34)', so at reach 26 the rack still meets the can. No value in long_slide's range clears 68 mm. Its rack sits outboard of the moving finger and its sector meshes from the outboard side, so as the jaw closes the drive moves away from the gap, not over it. The fingers are straight and vertical, so no pad reaches inward over a tall object's top. Sector radius 49.6 mm (opening about 93 mm, squeeze about 32 N, brief) covers sugar (92) and gives 32 N on the 514 g box. idea.name: outboard_rack_slide
idea.description: A long-travel slide jaw. The moving carriage rides two 3 x 150 mm steel rods on LM3UU bushings, like long_slide. Unlike long_slide, the module-1 rack is fixed to the carriage's outboard face, on the side away from the fixed jaw. The printed gear sector (pitch radius 49.6 mm, so 49.6 mm of finger travel per servo radian) meshes with it from the outboard side. When the jaw opens the rack extends outward, beyond the hand. When it closes the rack moves outward too, never into the space above the grasp gap. No drive member sits inside the gap at any opening, so the clearance above an object is limited only by the arm, not by a rack about 39–64 mm above the fingertips as on the stock long_slide. The moving finger is a straight vertical PLA blade, 40 mm below the carriage, with a 1 mm TPU face (friction 0.9). The fixed jaw gets a matching straight blade pad, so neither fingertip curves inward over an object's top. Faces stay parallel (0 deg) and the tip stays level (+1 mm) at every opening, from 17 mm (dice) to about 93 mm (sugar box).
idea.test: A simulator builder for a slide jaw whose rack and sector can be placed outboard of the carriage, or raised by a set clearance above the fingertip line. It needs straight vertical finger blades on both jaws, and a collision check of the drive against an object 84 mm tall (potted meat) and a 68 mm lying cylinder (tomato can) across the whole servo range -0.17..1.75 rad, including the wrist-interference check that refused sector 50 in iteration 10.

iterations.notes:
I'm proposing one new part and no trial, because I found no catalogue body that can gain a group without losing tomato_soup_can or banana.

**Why the catalogue is used up**
- **Current hinged jaw (revolute):** the numbers rule it out for the wide objects. At an 85 mm opening the moving fingertip sits 29 mm above the fixed one and its face is 52 deg off parallel, and the jaw opens to 90 mm at most. The pudding box (90 mm), sugar box (92) and mustard bottle (96) don't fit with clearance. Eight pad trials gained nothing. Tilting the pad to 36–45 deg loses the banana.
- **Parallelogram:** the fingertip still rises 48 mm at 85 mm. **Prismatic:** opens only 58 mm.
- **12 V servos:** refused at $68 against the $40 left. They wouldn't help anyway, because these failures are about geometry, not torque.
- **long_slide:** every slide body tried gains the pudding box, sugar box and tuna can, and every one loses the tomato can. The banana trial puts its rack about 39 mm above the table, so at most 39 mm above the fingertips at reach 5. Even the longest pad reach (30 mm) only takes that to 64 mm, below the lying tomato can's 68 mm top. That matches the iteration-10 log of the rack pressing on the can's top. Long reach also makes pads hit tall objects at the start: potted meat at t=0.02 s from reach 20, and apple at reach 26.

**What I'd rather not spend trials on**
- An untried pad reach around 12 mm on the slide might keep both the banana and the potted meat can. But my numbers say it still loses the tomato can, so it can't be kept. With three iterations left I'm not spending a trial on it.

**The new part: outboard_rack_slide**
- The slide's rack and gear sector sit on the outside of the moving finger, so nothing passes over the object at any opening. Both fingers are straight vertical blades.
- **Bill of materials:** 2 linear bushings ($2.40), 2 steel rods 3 x 150 mm ($4.00), M3 and M2 screws (on hand), 50 g PLA (250 min) and 2 g TPU (16 min).
- **Cost:** $6.40, 3 days of lead time, 266 machine minutes, which fits in $40, 7 days and 596 minutes.

**Overlap with past ideas**
- This is close to two ideas already recorded: long_slide_offset_sector (iteration 3) and long_slide_drop_finger (iteration 8).
- What it adds is the clearance rule: no part of the drive may sit lower than an object's top over the gap. It needs at least 68 mm for the tomato can, plus margin.
- It combines both earlier ideas into one part that a simulator builder could test.

If the simulator gets a builder for any of these three slide variants, that is the trial to run.

proposals.principle: A fingertip on a swinging joint rises by about R(1-cos q). Adding reach raises R, which lowers q for a given opening and widens the opening. A tilted contact squeezes the object out unless tan(a) < mu. pad_angle subtracts directly from the face tilt at a given opening.
proposals.hypothesis: The record varied reach (24-30, at pad angles 10-20) and pad angle (28-45, at reach 0) separately, never together at a small reach. proposals.mechanism: moving_jaw_on_top_face, with force_limit and fixed_jaw_missed as follow-ons: the moving face is fixed to the hinge, so at 85–96 mm it is tilted 52 deg or more with its bottom swung out (brief: 85 mm gives +52 deg, tip +29 mm). The contact moves to the top edge of the pad, which presses down on the object's top face (87 deg down for pudding and sugar).
proposals.principle: Two contacts hold an object only when their normals are horizontal and opposed. A face that turns with its joint is parallel at only one opening. A face free to turn about its own pin aligns itself to the object's wall at every opening, because a free pad can carry force only through its pin, so the pressure centre sits in front of the pin and the face lies flat on a vertical wall. Tip rise R(1−cos q) stays, but it only matters if the pin rises above the object's top.
proposals.hypothesis: Put a passive pivoting pad on the stock revolute jaw. The pad is free on a horizontal pin running across the jaw width, held centred by a weak printed TPU flexure, limited to ±30 deg, and pinned 6 mm above its lower edge with reach 0. At 85 mm the brief puts the moving tip +29 mm above the fixed tip. With the fixed tip about 3 mm above the table, the pin sits at about 32 mm and the pad face spans about 26–46 mm. On tuna (34 tall, vertical wall) it lies flat over 26–34 mm with a horizontal normal. Squeeze stays at 20 N, with TPU μ 0.9 against metal 0.35: 2×0.35×20 = 14 N against 1.7 N of weight. For pudding at 90 mm, extrapolated rise is about +34 mm, the pin is at about 37 and the contact band 31–38, under the 38 mm top. For sugar at 92 mm the pin is at about 40 and the band 34–45, under the 45 mm top. The arm then holds 0.41 + 0.15×5.14 = 1.18 N·m, below the 1.62 N·m stall. The opening is the binding limit. The bare stock jaw opens 99 mm. A 3.5 mm pivot pad on the moving jaw plus a 2.5 mm skin on the fixed jaw gives about 93 mm, against 90 mm with the current 5 mm pads. That fits tuna and pudding with room. Sugar at 92 mm is marginal, and mustard at 96 mm is out of reach. No catalogue part does this. pad_angle makes the face parallel at only one opening, and its 45 deg maximum still leaves +14 deg at 85 mm. Parallelogram and slides keep the face parallel, but they lift the tip 48 mm or bring the rack and sector into contact with tomato and potted meat.
risks: banana: rise at 70 mm is about +15 mm and the pad will align to the curved side. Small risk if the flexure is too weak and the pad hangs tilted on the descent; a ±30 deg stop and the centring flexure guard against it.

rolling objects (apple, tennis_ball, golf_ball, lemon, plum, strawberry, racquetball, tomato_soup_can): a free pad on a sphere puts its normal through the pin and the sphere's centre. If the pin is above the equator the push is downward, as it is now. The stock face already holds these, so I expect them to survive, but this is the main risk.
potted_meat_can and tomato_soup_can (heavy, metal μ 0.35): the TPU friction and 20 N squeeze are unchanged, and the self-aligned face removes tilt, so they should hold or improve.
dice, wood_block_cube, large_marker: at 17–26 mm the stock face is already within 2–4 deg of parallel, so the pad stays centred and behaves like today's pad.

idea.name: pivoting_self_aligning_pad
idea.description: A printed PLA pad carrier, 24 mm tall and 12–16 mm wide, with a 1 mm TPU skin (μ 0.9). It hangs on a horizontal pin through the bottom of the stock moving jaw: an M3 screw running in two MR63 bearings, pin 6 mm above the pad's lower edge, reach 0. A printed TPU flexure centres it, with hard stops at ±30 deg. The fixed jaw gets a thin flat pad, 1.5 mm PLA plus 1 mm TPU, so the opening stays at about 93 mm. Since the pad carries force only through its pin, its face rotates flat onto whatever wall it meets, so the contact normal is horizontal and opposed at every opening. That removes the moving face's tilt with its bottom swung out (+26 deg at 55 mm, +52 deg at 85 mm), which no pad_angle value cancels across the range, and it keeps the stock hinge's wide swing and no-rack geometry that the 17 held groups rely on.
idea.test: In the pads slot, add a passive hinge (revolute joint about the jaw-width axis) between the moving jaw and a pad body. Pin 6 mm above the pad's lower edge, joint limits ±30 deg, torsional stiffness about 0.02 N·m/rad (the TPU flexure), light damping. Pad face 24 mm tall with friction 0.9. Fixed-jaw pad 2.5 mm thick. Then rerun all 21 groups, with System 1 retuning side clearance and depth.

iterations.notes:
Diagnosis. Tuna (85 mm), pudding (90), sugar (92) and mustard (96) all fail for the same reason: the moving face is tilted, with its bottom swung out, at wide openings. With pads at 10 deg, the brief gives the face at +52 deg and the tip at +29 mm when the jaws are 85 mm apart. Because the bottom is swung out, the contact moves to the top edge of the pad, which lands on the object's top face. That is the logged 'moving_jaw_on_top_face' (87 deg down), or the force limit for tuna. The rva variants fail as 'fixed_jaw_missed': the 90 mm opening leaves almost no margin either side of an 85–92 mm object.

Why the catalogue is used up:
(a) Revolute pads: 10 parameter trials. The flattest face reachable is +14 deg at 85 mm (pad_angle 45), which still has its bottom swung out and lost the banana. Reach of 24 or more lost the tall objects. Combined angle and reach lost banana and potted meat.
(b) Parallelogram: the tip rises +48 mm at 85 mm with link 90.
(c) Prismatic: opens 58 mm at most.
(d) Long_slide gains pudding, sugar and tuna, but every variant lost tomato_soup_can. The sector stops at about 1.41 rad, which the interference refusal points to as the sector hitting the wrist, and the rack presses on the can's top at +33 mm. A sector radius above 44 mm also loses potted_meat_can. Pads shrink the slide's opening by about 2×(3 mm + TPU), so a sector radius of 44 mm or less cannot reach 92 mm with pads, and without pads the banana is lost. Those constraints conflict, and the 4-trial tuning rounds in iterations 4, 5 and 10 confirmed it.
(e) servos_12v is unaffordable ($68 against $40 left) and does not touch this mechanism anyway.

This is the last iteration but one. I am recording a new idea instead of repeating trials that are known to fail. Unlike the three earlier ideas, which were all slide variants, this one keeps the stock revolute jaw, so the held groups' geometry (no rack, no sector, stock swing) stays as it is. It removes the one quantity no pads parameter can remove: the face angle at wide openings.

To buy: 2 × mr63_bearing ($1.80 total, 3 days). A plain m3 screw from stock can serve as the pin at $0.

proposals.mechanism: moving_jaw_on_top_face (pudding, sugar, mustard, tuna). On the revolute jaw the hinge sits 81 mm above the fingertip. At 85 mm the face is 52 deg off parallel and the tip is +29 mm, and the jaw cannot open past 90 mm, so the pad lands on the top of a box 85 to 96 mm wide. The long_slide fixes face and tip (-10 deg with the current 10 deg pad angle, +1 mm), but its rack crosses the gap low down. It pressed on the top of the banana (38 tall) and the tomato can (68 tall), and its sector collided with the wrist at r=50. Raising the pads' reach to lift the rack cost us potted_meat_can and apple (a pad landed on their tops) at reach 8, 12, 20, 24 and 26. The slide is the right kind of joint, but its rack runs through the space the object needs.
proposals.principle: Two contacts hold an object only if their normals are horizontal and opposed, and only if the fingertip reaches below the object's top. A slide gives both at every opening. In the catalogue slide, the travel per radian (the sector radius r), the squeeze (torque/r) and the rack's depth below the servo axis (also r) are tied together. A compound gear stage separates them: travel = R1*(R3/r2), while the rack's height is set by where the output gear's axle is placed.
proposals.hypothesis: This is the last iteration and the catalogue is used up for these groups. Ten pads trials gained nothing. Every long_slide body lost tomato_soup_can, and every one with reach > 0 also lost potted_meat_can. On the slide, opening and rack clearance trade against each other: r=44 keeps potted but lets the rack hit the banana, and r>=46.7 loses potted. Parallelogram link 90 puts the tip at +48 mm at 85 mm, above every failing object's top (34 to 58 mm). Prismatic opens at most 58 mm. servos_12v costs $68 against $40 left. So no catalogue part or value fixes the mechanism, and I am recording one new part instead. The geared_high_rack_slide takes the slide's parallel, non-rising finger (the property behind b03t4's gains of mustard, pudding, sugar and tuna). It moves the rods and rack up to servo-axis height, behind the fixed-jaw line, and lets the finger hang on a straight drop leg. Nothing then crosses the gap below about 75 mm above the fingertips, so pads reach can stay at 0. Reach 0 is the only value that ever kept potted and apple, and the rack now clears banana (38) and tomato (68). Gear sizes: horn gear 40 teeth (R1=20 mm), idler 20 teeth (r2=10 mm) compounded with 50 teeth (R3=25 mm). That gives 50 mm/rad, about 96 mm of travel over the 1.92 rad servo range and about 29 N of squeeze after gear losses. The horn gear is only 21 mm in radius, so it clears the wrist where the r=50 sector did not.
risks: tomato_soup_can: the carriage at about 75 mm must stay above the lying can's 68 mm top across the grasp depths System 1 chooses. If it doesn't, the old rack-on-top failure comes back.
potted_meat_can: 84 tall, so it has to be grasped with the tip at about 15 mm or more so its top stays below the carriage. It held at reach 0, and this design keeps reach 0.
dice and large_marker: the slide must close to 17 mm with squeeze. The 96 mm of travel starts at the stop at -0.17 rad, so the closed gap has to be set at or below 10 mm when printed.
apple and tennis_ball: rounded tops below the carriage are fine, but the drop leg's stiffness under 29 N has to keep the face within a few degrees of vertical.

idea.name: geared_high_rack_slide
idea.description: A long slide with the rack lifted out of the gap. Two 3x150 mm steel rods in two LM3UU bushings carry the carriage, mounted level with the gripper servo axis, about 80 mm above the fingertips. A printed module-1 gear of 40 teeth (20 mm pitch radius) on the servo horn drives a printed compound idler on a 3 mm steel axle in two MR63 bearings. The idler's 20-tooth gear meshes the horn gear, and its 50-tooth gear drives the rack from below, with the rack teeth facing down. Finger travel is 20*(25/10) = 50 mm per servo radian, so about 96 mm over -0.17..1.75 rad. Squeeze is 1.62 N*m / 0.050 m = 32 N, about 29 N after mesh losses, enough for the 514 g sugar box (2*0.5*29 = 29 N against about 7.5 N with lift margin). The finger hangs from the carriage on a straight printed drop leg about 80 mm long. Its face stays vertical and its tip does not rise at any opening, and it carries the existing 2 mm TPU pads with pad_angle 0 and reach 0. The only part crossing the gap is the carriage itself, about 75 mm above the fingertip, so tall objects grasped at their equator (tomato 68 lying) or near the top (potted 84 upright, grasped shallow) are not touched. Added wrist mass is about 90 g, which puts the shoulder at about 0.41 + 0.77 (sugar) + 0.14 = 1.32 N*m against a 1.62 N*m stall.
idea.test: A simulator builder for a jaw whose rack and rails sit at a set height above the fingertip (rack_height_mm), with the finger on a drop leg and travel per radian set by a gear ratio, not by the sector radius. Run all 21 groups at rack_height 70, 80 and 90 mm and travel 48 to 52 mm/rad, pads reach 0 and pad_angle 0, and check banana, tomato, potted and apple first.

proposals.result: idea recorded, not tested: geared_high_rack_slide; it would need $9.70 from the manifest, 3 days, 258 machine min; within the budget left

iterations.notes:
I don't think any catalogue move can gain a group without losing one, so the one proposal this time is a new part (geared_high_rack_slide), recorded but not tested.

**Why the catalogue is used up:**
- **Pads on the hinged jaw:** 10 parameter trials gained nothing. Steep pad angles lost the banana, and any reach above 0 lost potted_meat_can (and apple).
- **long_slide:** every body lost tomato_soup_can because the rack sits too low. r=44 lets the rack hit the banana, r≥46.7 loses potted_meat_can, and r=50 collides with the wrist.
- **parallelogram:** at 85 mm the moving tip is +48 mm, above the top of every failing object.
- **prismatic:** opens at most 58 mm.
- **servos_12v:** costs $68 against $40 left.

**The new part:** a slide whose rack sits above the gap. A small horn gear drives a compound idler, so the finger travels 50 mm per radian (about 96 mm opening, about 29 N squeeze), while the rack sits about 75 mm up and the finger hangs on a straight leg. Pads reach stays at 0.

**Cost:** $9.70 to buy (LM3UU ×2, 3×150 rod ×2, MR63 ×2, 3×100 rod ×1), 3 days lead time, about 258 machine minutes. That is within $40, 7 days and 596 minutes. Screws are on hand.

**Main risk:** whether the carriage at about 75 mm clears the 68 mm tomato can.
